questions.stem: Which part of a neuron carries impulses away from the cell body?
options: The dendrites
The nucleus
The node of Ranvier only
The axon
questions.explanation: The axon conducts impulses away from the cell body towards the axon terminals. Dendrites receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body.

questions.stem: What is the function of the myelin sheath around many axons?
options: It insulates the axon and speeds up the conduction of impulses
It produces the neurotransmitter that is released at the synapse
It receives impulses from receptors and passes them to the axon
It supplies the axon with glucose from the cerebrospinal fluid
questions.explanation: Myelin is a fatty insulating layer formed by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. Because it insulates the axon, the impulse jumps between the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), which is much faster than conduction along an unmyelinated fibre.

questions.stem: What is a reflex?
options: A rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought
A learned response that becomes faster each time the stimulus is repeated
A slow response to a stimulus that is brought about by hormones in the blood
A voluntary response that is planned in the cerebrum before muscles contract
questions.explanation: A reflex is a fast, involuntary and usually protective response, such as pulling a hand away from a hot object. It is not learned and does not require conscious decision.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of a simple reflex arc?
options: Receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, motor neuron, interneuron, sensory neuron, effector
Effector, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, receptor
Receptor, interneuron, sensory neuron, motor neuron, effector
questions.explanation: A receptor detects the stimulus, a sensory neuron carries the impulse to the CNS, an interneuron passes it on, and a motor neuron carries it to the effector, which responds.

questions.stem: Where is the interneuron of a spinal withdrawal reflex located?
options: In the white matter of the cerebrum
In the dorsal root ganglion outside the cord
In the skin, next to the pain receptor
In the grey matter of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Interneurons lie entirely within the CNS. In a spinal reflex the interneuron is in the grey matter of the spinal cord, linking the sensory neuron to the motor neuron. The dorsal root ganglion contains sensory neuron cell bodies.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a sensory neuron from a motor neuron?
options: It has no myelin sheath, so its impulses travel much more slowly
It carries impulses away from the CNS to muscles and glands
Its cell body lies to one side of the fibre, in a ganglion outside the CNS
Its cell body lies at one end of the fibre, inside the grey matter of the CNS
questions.explanation: A sensory neuron has its cell body set off to the side of the long fibre, in a dorsal root ganglion. A motor neuron's cell body is in the grey matter of the CNS, with many dendrites and a long axon leading to the effector.

questions.stem: A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before feeling any pain. Why is the movement made before the pain is felt?
options: Motor neurons conduct impulses faster than sensory neurons conduct impulses
The reflex is coordinated in the spinal cord; impulses to the brain arrive later
Pain receptors do not respond until after the muscles have already contracted
The brain processes the pain first but delays the sensation until the hand moves
questions.explanation: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord, so the response does not wait for the brain. Impulses also travel up the cord to the cerebrum, and the pain is felt once they arrive and are interpreted.

questions.stem: Why are reflexes important for survival?
options: They replace the need for hormones in long-term regulation
They let the body learn new skills by repeating each movement
They produce fast responses that protect the body from harm
They allow responses to be planned before any action is taken
questions.explanation: Reflexes are rapid and automatic, so they quickly remove the body from danger, protect the airways and help maintain posture. Their speed comes from having few synapses and no conscious processing.

questions.stem: In the knee-jerk reflex, the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron in the spinal cord. How does this compare with a withdrawal reflex that includes an interneuron?
options: The knee jerk is conscious, because the interneuron is replaced by the brain
The knee jerk uses no effector, because the motor neuron acts as the muscle
The knee jerk is faster, because the impulse crosses fewer synapses
The knee jerk is slower, because it lacks an interneuron to boost the signal
questions.explanation: Each synapse adds a short delay while neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap. With only one synapse, the knee-jerk reflex is faster than a reflex that passes through an interneuron. Neither reflex requires the brain.

questions.stem: A patient's skin can still feel a pin-prick on the foot, but the leg does not move when the reflex is tested, although the muscles are healthy. Where is the damage most likely to be?
options: In the cerebrum, where sensations are felt
In the motor neurons supplying the leg muscles
In the sensory neurons from the skin of the foot
In the pain receptors in the skin of the foot
questions.explanation: Feeling the pin-prick shows the receptors, sensory neurons and pathway to the brain are working. If the healthy muscle does not respond, the fault lies in the efferent part of the arc, the motor neurons. Damage to the cerebrum would not stop a spinal reflex.

questions.stem: A microelectrode placed inside a resting neuron reads about -70 mV compared with the outside. What does this reading show?
options: The neuron is in the middle of firing an action potential
Sodium ions are more concentrated inside than outside the cell
The inside of the membrane is negative relative to the outside
The inside of the membrane is positive relative to the outside
questions.explanation: At rest, the inside of a neuron is about 70 millivolts negative compared with the outside. This resting potential is maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and the membrane's greater permeability to potassium ions, and sodium is more concentrated outside.

questions.stem: A weak stimulus raises a neuron's membrane potential from -70 mV to -62 mV, and it then returns to rest with no action potential. What best explains this?
options: The neuron was already firing, so it could not respond to another stimulus
The stimulus opened potassium channels, which made the inside more positive
The sodium-potassium pump moved sodium into the cell faster than usual
The change did not reach the threshold needed to open enough sodium channels
questions.explanation: An action potential starts only when depolarisation reaches threshold, roughly -55 mV, at which point many voltage-gated sodium channels open. A smaller change fades away. Opening potassium channels would make the inside more negative, not more positive.

questions.stem: How does the sodium-potassium pump help maintain the resting potential?
options: It moves chloride ions into the cell whenever the neuron is stimulated
It uses ATP to move three sodium ions out for every two potassium ions in
It uses ATP to move three potassium ions out for every two sodium ions in
It lets sodium and potassium ions diffuse freely in both directions
questions.explanation: The pump actively transports three Na⁺ out of the cell and two K⁺ in, using ATP. This keeps sodium concentrated outside and potassium inside, and contributes to the inside being negative.

questions.stem: What happens at the axon membrane during depolarisation?
options: Potassium channels open and potassium ions rush into the axon
Sodium channels close and sodium ions are pumped out of the axon
Potassium channels open and potassium ions flow out of the axon
Sodium channels open and sodium ions rush into the axon
questions.explanation: When the membrane reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in, making the inside positive. The outflow of K⁺ through potassium channels happens next, during repolarisation.

questions.stem: What causes repolarisation of the axon membrane after the peak of an action potential?
options: Calcium ions enter the axon and cancel out the positive charge inside
Potassium ions flow out of the axon through opened potassium channels
Sodium ions flow out of the axon through opened sodium channels
Potassium ions are pumped into the axon by the opened potassium channels
questions.explanation: At the peak, sodium channels close and potassium channels open. K⁺ diffuses out, so the inside becomes negative again. The sodium-potassium pump then restores the original ion distribution.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a nerve impulse is all-or-none?
options: Once threshold is reached, an action potential of full size is produced
Every neuron in a nerve fires whenever any one of the neurons is stimulated
A stronger stimulus produces a larger action potential in the same neuron
An impulse either reaches the brain or is converted into a hormone instead
questions.explanation: A stimulus below threshold produces no action potential, while any stimulus at or above threshold produces one of the same size. Action potentials do not get bigger with a stronger stimulus.

questions.stem: A light touch and a firm press on the skin both produce action potentials in the same sensory neuron. How does the nervous system tell the strength of the two stimuli apart?
options: The firm press produces action potentials that travel faster
The firm press produces action potentials that last longer
The firm press produces more action potentials per second
The firm press produces taller action potentials each time
questions.explanation: Because action potentials are all-or-none, their size cannot carry information about intensity. A stronger stimulus instead produces a higher frequency of impulses, and may stimulate more receptors.

questions.stem: A recording from an axon shows the membrane potential at -70 mV, rising sharply to about +35 mV, then falling briefly below -70 mV before settling. What explains the brief dip below the resting value?
options: Chloride ions leave the axon as soon as the sodium channels close
Potassium channels stay open a little too long, so extra K⁺ leaves
Sodium channels stay open a little too long, so extra Na⁺ enters
The sodium-potassium pump stops working, so ions leak across
questions.explanation: The dip is hyperpolarisation. The potassium channels close slowly, so slightly more K⁺ leaves than is needed to restore the resting potential, making the inside briefly more negative. Extra Na⁺ entering would make the inside more positive.

questions.stem: Why does a nerve impulse travel in only one direction along an axon?
options: The membrane just behind the impulse is in its refractory period
Sodium ions can diffuse in only one direction along the axon
The myelin sheath blocks any impulse travelling back to the cell body
Neurotransmitter pushes the impulse forward from behind
questions.explanation: Immediately after an action potential, that part of the membrane cannot fire again for a short time (the refractory period). So the local currents can only trigger the next region ahead, and the impulse moves away from where it started.

questions.stem: What is saltatory conduction?
options: The impulse travelling continuously along every part of an unmyelinated axon
The impulse crossing a synapse by the diffusion of a chemical neurotransmitter
The impulse being boosted by salt in the cerebrospinal fluid around the axon
The impulse jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon
questions.explanation: In myelinated axons, action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. The impulse jumps from node to node, so it travels much faster than along an unmyelinated axon.

questions.stem: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system damages the myelin sheaths of neurons in the CNS. Which effect would you predict?
options: Slower or blocked conduction of impulses along the affected axons
Faster conduction of impulses, because the insulation has been removed
Larger action potentials, because more sodium can enter along the axon
No change in conduction, because myelin only protects the axon physically
questions.explanation: Without myelin, impulses can no longer jump from node to node, so conduction slows or fails, producing symptoms such as weakness and loss of coordination. Action potential size is all-or-none and does not increase.

questions.stem: Which axon would conduct impulses fastest?
options: A small-diameter unmyelinated axon
A large-diameter myelinated axon
A small-diameter myelinated axon
A large-diameter unmyelinated axon
questions.explanation: Both myelination and a larger diameter increase conduction speed, so a wide myelinated axon is fastest. Myelination has the greater effect, which is why it is so common in vertebrate nerves.

questions.stem: What is the synaptic cleft?
options: The channel through which sodium ions enter the axon during an impulse
The narrow gap between an axon terminal and the next cell
The space between two neighbouring nodes of Ranvier along an axon
The fluid-filled space between the meninges surrounding the brain
questions.explanation: The synaptic cleft is the small gap that separates the presynaptic axon terminal from the postsynaptic membrane of a neuron, muscle fibre or gland cell. The signal crosses it chemically.

questions.stem: What triggers the release of neurotransmitter when an impulse arrives at an axon terminal?
options: The neurotransmitter diffusing out through channels in the axon membrane
Calcium ions entering, causing vesicles to fuse with the membrane
Sodium ions leaving the terminal, causing vesicles to burst inside the cell
Potassium ions entering the terminal, causing the membrane to break down
questions.explanation: Depolarisation of the terminal opens calcium channels. Ca²⁺ enters and causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents into the cleft by exocytosis.

questions.stem: What happens after neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the synaptic cleft?
options: They bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels
They enter the postsynaptic cell and travel along its axon as the impulse
They bind to the myelin sheath of the next neuron and speed up conduction
They return to the presynaptic vesicles before any response is produced
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter binds specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane. In an excitatory synapse this opens sodium channels and depolarises the membrane, which can start a new action potential.

questions.stem: A neuron is stimulated artificially halfway along its axon. Impulses travel both ways along the axon, but only those reaching the axon terminal pass to the next neuron. Why?
options: Transmitter is released only presynaptically, and receptors are only postsynaptic
Neurotransmitter can only diffuse downhill from the dendrites of one neuron towards the next cell body
The postsynaptic membrane is myelinated, which stops impulses passing back towards the axon terminal
The synaptic cleft contains valves that close behind the neurotransmitter once it has moved across
questions.explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are found only in the axon terminal, and the matching receptors only on the postsynaptic membrane, so the chemical signal can pass one way only. This keeps information flowing in a set direction through a pathway.

questions.stem: Why must neurotransmitter be removed from the synaptic cleft soon after it is released?
options: Otherwise the cleft would fill with myelin and block transmission
Otherwise the neurotransmitter would travel back up the axon
Otherwise the postsynaptic cell would keep being stimulated
Otherwise the presynaptic neuron would run out of sodium ions
questions.explanation: Enzymes such as acetylcholinesterase break neurotransmitter down, or it is taken back up into the terminal. Removing it ends each signal, so the postsynaptic cell responds only while impulses keep arriving.

questions.stem: Some insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine at synapses with muscles. What effect would poisoning with such a chemical have?
options: Muscles would contract more weakly, because receptors are blocked
Muscles would be unaffected, because acetylcholine breaks down by itself
Muscles would contract continuously, because acetylcholine stays bound
Muscles would fail to contract, because no acetylcholine is released
questions.explanation: If acetylcholinesterase cannot work, acetylcholine builds up in the cleft and keeps stimulating the muscle fibres, causing twitching and spasms. Blocking release or blocking receptors would cause paralysis instead.

questions.stem: Transmission across a synapse is slower than conduction along an axon. What best explains this?
options: Synapses can transmit an impulse only once the axon has fully repolarised
Crossing the cleft depends on release, diffusion and binding of a chemical
Crossing the cleft requires a much larger action potential to be produced
Synapses are unmyelinated, so impulses travel along them by saltatory conduction
questions.explanation: At a synapse the electrical signal is converted to a chemical one: vesicles must release neurotransmitter, which diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors. These steps take longer than an action potential moving along the membrane, causing synaptic delay.

questions.stem: Some neurotransmitters make the postsynaptic membrane more negative inside. What is the effect of this?
options: It makes the postsynaptic neuron fire an impulse immediately
It makes the impulse travel backwards to the presynaptic neuron
It makes the postsynaptic neuron less likely to fire an impulse
It makes the postsynaptic neuron fire a larger impulse than usual
questions.explanation: An inhibitory neurotransmitter moves the membrane further from threshold, so the neuron is less likely to produce an action potential. Inhibitory synapses help prevent unwanted responses and allow fine control.

questions.stem: How does the speed of action of the nervous system compare with that of the endocrine system?
options: Hormonal responses are faster because blood flows more quickly than impulses travel
Nervous responses usually occur within milliseconds; hormonal responses take seconds to hours
Nervous responses usually take hours to develop; hormonal responses occur within milliseconds
Both systems usually respond at the same speed because both rely on chemical messengers
questions.explanation: Nerve impulses travel rapidly along neurons and across synapses, so responses are almost immediate. Hormones must be secreted, carried in the blood and act on target cells, which takes longer.

questions.stem: How do the messages of the nervous and endocrine systems differ in how they are transmitted?
options: Nervous: chemicals in the blood plasma; endocrine: impulses along the cranial nerves
Nervous: electrochemical impulses along neurons; endocrine: hormones carried in the blood
Nervous: hormones carried along neurons; endocrine: electrical impulses carried in the blood
Nervous: chemicals in the lymph vessels; endocrine: impulses along the spinal cord
questions.explanation: The nervous system sends electrochemical impulses along neurons, with chemical transmission at synapses. The endocrine system releases hormones that travel in the blood to all parts of the body.

questions.stem: Compared with a nervous response, how long does a hormonal response usually last?
options: Shorter, because hormones act only while nerve impulses are arriving
Longer, because hormones stay in the blood until they are broken down
Shorter, because hormones are broken down within a few milliseconds
The same, because both stop the moment the stimulus is detected
questions.explanation: Nervous responses usually stop soon after the impulses stop. Hormones remain in the blood until they are broken down, and some, such as growth hormone, act over months or years.

questions.stem: At the junction between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre, which neurotransmitter is released?
options: Acetylcholine
Adrenaline
Dopamine
Insulin
questions.explanation: Motor neurons release acetylcholine, which binds receptors on the muscle fibre and triggers contraction. The junction works like a synapse between two neurons. Insulin is a hormone, not a neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: Why is the nervous system said to be more specific in its effects than the endocrine system?
options: Neurons signal particular effector cells; hormones reach every cell with the receptor
Neurons release their signals into the blood, while hormones are delivered to one cell at a time
Neurons act on every body cell at once, while hormones act only on the cells of a single gland
Neurons use many different neurotransmitters, while all hormones share one type of receptor
questions.explanation: A motor neuron synapses with particular muscle fibres or gland cells, so its effect is localised. A hormone in the blood reaches the whole body and affects all cells that have its receptors, which may be in many tissues.

questions.stem: A sudden fright makes a person's heart race within a second, and it stays fast for several minutes after the danger has passed. Which explanation is best?
options: Sympathetic nerves act first, then aldosterone from the adrenal cortex prolongs the effect
Sympathetic nerves act first, then adrenaline from the adrenal medulla prolongs the effect
Adrenaline acts first, then the parasympathetic nerves prolong the raised heart rate
The cerebellum acts first, then insulin from the pancreas prolongs the raised heart rate
questions.explanation: Sympathetic nerves raise the heart rate almost immediately, and they also stimulate the adrenal medulla to secrete adrenaline. Adrenaline stays in the blood for some time, so the effect outlasts the nerve signals. This shows the two systems working together.

questions.stem: The nervous and endocrine systems are said to work together. Which example best shows this?
options: The pancreas releases insulin after it detects a rise in glucose in the blood
The hypothalamus detects low water levels and causes ADH release from the pituitary
The cerebellum adjusts muscle tone so that posture is held while a person stands
The medulla increases the breathing rate after a rise in carbon dioxide in the blood
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, part of the nervous system, trigger the release of a hormone, ADH, that acts on the kidneys. The other examples involve only one system each.
